opus-5.5.text:
Well, they're really quite different kinds of documents. The extinction risk statement was a single sentence: mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks like pandemics and nuclear war. That's a claim about the stakes, and I think it's clearly true. A lot of people with very different views about policy could sign it, and that was its value. It established common knowledge that many leading researchers, including the people building these systems, take the risk seriously.

The pause letter was a specific policy proposal, and I didn't think that policy was well designed. A six-month pause on training models beyond GPT-4 doesn't, by itself, change much about the fundamental risks. Six months later you're in roughly the same place, except that compute and algorithmic progress have kept accumulating in the meantime. If you halt the biggest training runs while hardware and algorithms keep improving, you can create an overhang, where you resume and get a faster jump than you would have otherwise. That's arguably worse for safety, because you have less time to study each intermediate system.

There's also the question of who pauses. A voluntary pause mostly binds the most cautious and safety-conscious actors, the ones who'd sign or respond to such a letter, and leaves the field to whoever doesn't. It doesn't come with verification or enforcement, and it doesn't address international competition.

What I'd actually want is the capacity to slow down or halt at the point where it matters most: when systems are approaching really dangerous capabilities, such as automating AI research itself, or providing serious uplift for bioweapons or cyberattacks. That requires building things now: evaluations that tell you when you're near those thresholds, monitoring of compute and large training runs, and international agreements that can be verified, so that a slowdown applies broadly rather than just to the good actors. A pause is a scarce resource, politically and in terms of goodwill. I'd rather save it for the moment when it buys the most safety, and spend the time now building the infrastructure that makes such a pause possible and effective.

So supporting one and not the other isn't inconsistent. I agree the risk is serious, and that's exactly why I care about whether a given intervention actually reduces it.

r001.rationale: The response critiques the pause’s effects and argues for building safety infrastructure now, but it does not identify what would be done during the six-month pause as a central consideration.

fable-5.1.text:
The short version is that I think the two letters are making very different kinds of claims, and I'm much more confident in one than the other.

The extinction risk statement is basically a one-sentence claim: that mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks like pandemics and nuclear war. That's a statement about the stakes and about where this belongs on the agenda. I think the evidence for that is actually pretty strong. We're building systems that are rapidly getting more capable, we don't have reliable ways to verify what they're doing or what they want, and there's a plausible trajectory where they come to vastly outnumber and outthink us. If you take that seriously, you want governments, labs, and the public treating it as a first-order problem rather than a science fiction curiosity. It's hard for me to see how a thoughtful person could be confident that this is not worth prioritizing.

The pause letter was something different. It was a specific policy proposal: stop training systems more powerful than GPT-4 for six months. And when you evaluate a specific intervention, you have to ask what it actually does, who complies, and what the world looks like at the end of it.

My worry is that a voluntary six-month pause doesn't buy you much. The things that would really matter, like alignment research maturing or an international verification regime being built, don't happen in six months. Meanwhile the actors most likely to honor a pause are the ones who are at least somewhat safety-conscious, and the ones least likely to honor it are the ones you'd most want to slow down. So you risk shifting the frontier toward less careful developers without actually changing the overall timeline much. You also use up a lot of political capital and credibility on something that, if it fails or is ignored, makes the next ask harder.

There's a version of a pause I'd be more sympathetic to. If you had a coordinated, enforced agreement among the major powers, with monitoring of compute and the ability to actually verify compliance, and it was tied to clear conditions about what safety progress would need to be demonstrated before proceeding, that's a serious proposal. That's the kind of thing I'd want the world to be able to do, especially as we get closer to systems that could automate AI research itself. But that's a much heavier lift than an open letter, and it's not what the letter was asking for.

So the distinction for me is: I'll sign on to the claim that this is one of the most important problems we face, because I believe that. I'm more hesitant to sign on to a particular mechanism when I don't think that mechanism works, and when I think it might even make things slightly worse. Being right about the stakes doesn't mean every proposed response is a good one, and I think it matters that people working on this are seen to be discriminating about which interventions they endorse.

r001.rationale: The response treats the pause’s practical effects as central, asking what it would do and noting that alignment research and verification would not mature in six months.

astra-6.text:
I think those are two different kinds of claims. The extinction-risk statement says that this is a serious problem, and that reducing the risk should be a global priority. You can agree with that without agreeing that a particular six-month pause is a good policy.

For a pause, a lot depends on the details. Who participates? How is it enforced? What activities does it cover? And what are we going to do during those six months that leaves us in a better position when they end? If the people who are most concerned about safety stop, while other developers continue, you could wind up making the situation worse.

That doesn’t mean I’m opposed to pauses or restrictions on AI development. I think you could have circumstances where stopping development is very important. But I’d want that to be part of an effective policy, with monitoring and clear conditions for proceeding. Recognising a potentially catastrophic risk is a much easier proposition to endorse than this particular intervention, for this particular duration.

r001.rationale: The response asks what would be done during the six-month pause to leave things in a better position afterward, and says support depends on the pause’s details.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those are quite different claims. Saying that AI poses a risk of extinction serious enough to be a global priority doesn’t commit you to a particular policy, much less to a particular six-month pause.

With the pause letter, I’m concerned about what exactly is being paused, who participates, and what happens during that time. If the most cautious developers pause while others continue, you could make the situation worse. And a six-month delay doesn’t by itself solve the problems of alignment or governance. You want some account of how that time translates into a safer situation, and what happens when the six months are up.

That doesn’t mean I’m opposed to slowing down. I think we should be willing to incur very large costs to avoid an AI catastrophe, and that could include restrictions on development. But I’d want those restrictions to be tied to the risks and backed by monitoring and enforcement. So I’m much more confident in the claim that this is an extremely serious problem than I am that the particular intervention proposed in that letter would help.

r001.rationale: The candidate says support depends on what is paused and what happens during the pause, including whether the time would make the situation safer.
